html:
Sheep, and later cattle, reached the far south of Africa around 2,000 years ago. The herders who kept them became the Khoekhoe, who lived alongside San hunter-gatherers around the Cape.

How herding arrived is still argued. Some evidence points to a small movement of herders from East Africa, where herding had spread long before. Other evidence suggests that local hunter-gatherers took up sheep through trade. Genetic studies find a trace of East African ancestry in Khoekhoe people, so both may be true. Pottery and sheep bones appear at Cape sites about the same time.

The Khoekhoe moved with their herds between seasonal pastures and lived in clans. In the east they met Bantu-speaking farmers of the Bantu expansion, such as the ancestors of the Xhosa.

When the Dutch settled the Cape in 1652 they bought cattle from the Khoekhoe, then took their grazing land. Wars and the smallpox epidemic of 1713 broke Khoekhoe independence.
sum: Sheep, and later cattle, reached the far south of Africa around 2,000 years ago. The herders who kept them became the Khoekhoe, who lived alongside San hunter-gatherers around the Cape.
